text:
Investors are betting on more upside in US Treasuries.

The extra cost investors are willing to pay for call options on longer-dated Treasuries relative to puts is up to ~50 basis points, the highest since March 2025.

This marks a sharp reversal from a 250-basis-point premium for puts over calls in late September.

This suggests investors are increasingly betting on further gains in Treasury prices.

Furthermore, one options trade is targeting a drop in the 10Y Note Yield to ~4.60% within a month, involving ~65,000 contracts and costing ~$7 million in premium.

This comes as the 10Y Note Yield has declined below 5.00% for the first time since September 23rd, now down -40 basis points from the October 7th peak.

The bond market is seeing massive swings in price and sentiment.

en_summary: @SawyerMerritt: AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile are jointly lobbying the FCC to keep existing rules as SpaceX nears launching its own cellular network; their reps met FCC officials on Oct 20. $T $VZ $TMUS $SPCX
text:
AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile are jointly lobbying the FCC to preserve existing rules as @SpaceX moves closer to launching its own independent cellular network that would compete directly with the three major U.S. carriers.

On Oct 20th, reps from all three major U.S. wireless carriers met with FCC officials to push back against proposed changes that would give satellite companies more freedom to offer cellular service.

The carriers urged the FCC to:
• Block satellite companies from using certain 5G frequencies currently used by wireless carriers.
• Keep rules requiring satellite companies to get permission from wireless carriers before using their licensed spectrum.
• Allow wireless carriers to maintain control over these agreements, including the ability to end them.
• Reconsider proposed interference limits to protect existing cellular networks.

Based on all the public communications from these carriers, and the lobbying, they are clearly worried that SpaceX's @Starlink Mobile network is going to be a major competitor to them. Starlink Mobile will become the first network operator to deploy both satellite and terrestrial spectrum.

The FCC recently announced that they are considering new rules that could make it easier for satellite companies like SpaceX to offer cellular service without relying as heavily on existing wireless carriers, so this is partly what the three big carriers are fighting against.

en_summary: @SawyerMerritt: NHTSA proposed rules to remove federal barriers for autonomous vehicles without steering wheels or pedals, such as Tesla's Cybercab, including dropping manual turn signal control requirements.
text:
NHTSA announced today that they are proposing new rules aimed at removing U.S. federal regulatory barriers for autonomous vehicles without steering wheels or pedals, such as @Tesla's Cybercab.

The proposed changes include:
• Eliminating requirements for manually operated turn signal controls in vehicles without steering wheels or pedals: "NHTSA has concluded that the self-canceling and manually operated control requirements in the current standard are unnecessary for turn signal operating units that are installed on vehicles without manually operated driving controls."

• Allowing autonomous driving systems to control turn signals, hazard lights, and high/low beams without traditional driver-operated switches.

• Removing certain dashboard indicator requirements for turn signals and high beams in vehicles without manual driving controls.

• Allowing optional cyan-colored exterior lights to indicate when a vehicle is operating autonomously, with standardized requirements for their placement, brightness, and operation.

• Eliminating outdated restrictions on vertical headlight arrangements, giving automakers greater design flexibility.

• Allowing modern integrated headlights to be tested at manufacturer-specified voltages rather than requiring 12.8 volts.

NHTSA says the changes are intended to eliminate unnecessary regulatory barriers, reduce costs, and enable innovation without compromising vehicle safety.

- Tech-focused hedge funds: down ~10% in October

There’s separate interviews where Citadel/JP Morgan have been saying retail has been the ones buying the dip in semiconductor, neocloud, and memory stocks.

Reuters stated this downturn triggered institutional deleveraging events among hedge funds.

Quite the divergence, I do think there’s been a ton of irrational selling now, hedge fund deleveraging seems to be a major contributor.

zh_summary: @aleabitoreddit: $NVDA Jensen Huang told CNBC a memory oversupply by 2029 is unlikely because you can always use more memory, citing LPDDR use in data centers, rebutting a Korean view of a 2029 red ocean.
en_summary: @aleabitoreddit: $NVDA Jensen Huang told CNBC a memory oversupply by 2029 is unlikely because you can always use more memory, citing LPDDR use in data centers, rebutting a Korean view of a 2029 red ocean.
text:
$NVDA Jensen Huang: Surplus of memory supply is unlikely by 2029. 

The CNBC question referenced a Korean newspaper opinion on $KOSPI / Samsung / SK Hynix that predicted "new supply will leave the memory sector a red ocean in 2029."

"One of the things that's really great about memory is that you can always use more of it", Jensen said, citing LPDDR usage in DCs.  And responded "I don't think so" in terms of possibilities of oversupply in 2029. 

Just my personal opinion, Nvidia probably has the most visibility in the entire industry. 

Especially around supply procurement and emerging capacity, given they're the ones leading all the architectural shifts. 

On durability, you have Samsung already allocated majority of capacity into 2031 from SED and hyperscalers like $GOOGL are already reportedly securing memory LTAs into 2035 from KeyBanc. 

Yet there's endless "it's all over" sentiment on memory now. I'd probably trust Jensen's opinion here.
